Chapter 5





                                                                5-1

1. Explain how the consumer price index (CPI) is
   constructed and use it to calculate the inflation
   rate
2. Show how the CPI is used to adjust dollar
   amounts to eliminate the effects of inflation
3. Discuss the important biases in the CPI
4. Distinguish between inflation and relative price
   changes to find the true costs of inflation
5. Summarize the connections among inflation,
   nominal interest rates, and real interest rates

                                                                            3

• Prices of goods change over time
  – When the world used metallic money (gold,
     silver) prices sometimes increased sharply,
    and sometimes decreased sharply
  – Since the advent of fiat money, prices have
     generally steadily increased
• To compare over time, economists try to
  adjust dollar values to compensate for
  price changes (inflation)


                                                                                                           5-4
                                                                         4

• A price index measures the average price of a
  given class of good or services relative to the price
  of the same goods and services in a base year
   – Inflation is measured as the rate of growth of the price
     index
• CPI measures the change in consumer prices
• Other indices:
   – Core inflation is CPI without energy and food
   – Producer price index: prices of intermediate goods
   – GDP Deflator: (Nominal GDP/Real GDP)×100
   – Import / export price index
                                                                                                           5-5
                                                                         5

• The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a
  measure of the cost of living during a
  particular period
• The CPI measures
  – The cost of a standard basket of goods
    and services in a given year
  – relative to the cost of the same basket of
    goods and services in the base year


                                                                                                       5-6
                                                                       6

From “Are Chinese Growth and Inflation Too Smooth? Evidence
from Engel Curves”, Nakamura, Steinsson, and Liu (2016)

                                                                5-8
                                             8

1. Fix the “basket.”
   The government (National Bureau of Statistics
    of China, or Bureau of Labor Statistics in US)
   surveys consumers to determine what’s in the
    typical consumer’s “shopping basket.”
2. Find the prices.
   They collect data on the prices of all the
   goods in the basket.
3. Compute the basket’s cost.
   Use the prices to compute the total cost of the
   basket.

 E.g. 2010 is the base year for the CPI

• CPI is the ratio of the cost of the basket of goods in the
  current year to the cost in the base year
  – Base year cost $680
  – 2015 cost $850
              CPI = 850 / 680 = 1.25
• Cost of living in 2015 is 25% higher than in 2010
  – CPI for the base year is always 1
  – CPI for a given period is the cost of living in that
     period relative to what it was in the base year
  – BEA uses CPI as a percentage – the ratio times 100

                                                                                                   5-16
                                                                        16

• A nominal quantity is measured in terms of
   its current dollar value
• A real quantity is measured in physical terms
  – Quantities of goods and services
• To compare values over time, use real
  quantities
  – Deflating a nominal quantity converts it to a real
     quantity  inflation-adjusted quantities
         • Divide a nominal quantity by its price index to express
         the quantity in real terms                                               5-17
                                                                         17

• Can a family buy more with $40,000 in income in
  2010 or with $44,000 in 2015?
   – 2010 is the base year for the CPI
   – Deflate nominal income in both years to get real
     income
   – Compare real income
   – $40,000 in 2010 has the greater purchasing power

Year   Nominal Income   CPI          Real Income
2010       $40,000        1.00      $40,000/1.00 = $40,000
2015       $44,000        1.25      $44,000/1.25 = $35,200

• The real wage is the wage paid to the worker
  measured in terms of purchasing power
      Real wage for any given period =
      the nominal wage / CPI for that period
• U.S. production worker wages
   – CPI uses 1983 as base year
   – Real wages stayed roughly the same between 1970 and 2013
      despite the fact that the nominal wage in 2013 was almost 6
      times the nominal wage in 1970
    Year    Average Wage    CPI       Real Average Wage
   1970        $3.40         0.39        $3.40 / 0.39 = $8.72
   2013       $20.14        2.29       $20.14 / 2.29 = $8.79

Base Year 1983





                                                                        5-21
                                                     21

• Indexing increases a nominal quantity each period
  by the percentage increase in a specified price
  index
   – Indexing prevents the purchasing power of the nominal
      quantity from being eroded by inflation
• Indexing automatically adjusts certain values, such
  as Social Security payments, by the amount of
   inflation
   – If prices increase 3% in a given year, the Social
     Security recipients receive 3% more
          • No action by Congress required
   – Indexing is sometimes included in labor contracts                                                                                                      5-22
                                                                          22

• An indexed labor contract
   – First year wage is $12 per hour
   – Employer guarantees that real wages rise by 2% per
     year for the next 2 years
   – Relevant price index is 1.00 in first year, 1.05 in the
     second, and 1.10 in the third
• Nominal wage is real wage times the price index
  Year  Real Wage  Price Index  Nominal Wage
  1       $12.00       1.00          $12.00
  2       $12.24       1.05          $12.85
  3       $12.48       1.10          $13.73
                                                                                                     5-23
                                                                         23

• CPI and other indexes influence policy decisions
  and wage increases
• 1996 report said CPI overstates inflation by 1 to 2
  percentage points a year in the U.S.
   – Unnecessarily increases government spending
          • Social Welfare payments and many contracts have COLAs
           (cost-of-living-allowance) tied to the CPI
   – Underestimates increase in the standard of living
          • Suppose CPI indicates 3% inflation when cost of living
           actually increases 2%
          • Real income increased by 1% more than estimated
• Since 1996, CPI calculations changed to improve
                                                                                                     5-24  the accuracy of the CPI in estimating inflation                                                                         24

• CPI uses a fixed basket of goods and services
   – When the price of a good increases, consumers buy less
     and substitute other goods
   – Failing to account for substitution overstates inflation
• Example: base year cost of market basket
   – Suppose that people like coffee and tea equally well
   Item             2010 price    2010 Spending
   Coffee (50 cups)      $1.00          $50.00
   Tea (50 cups)         $1.00          $50.00
   Scones (100)         $1.00         $100.00

                                                                                                      5-25   Total                              $200.00
                                                                         25

• In 2015, coffee and scones are more expensive
  – Buying exactly the same basket of goods costs
    $300, compared to $200 in 2005
  – CPI = 300 / 200 = 1.50

    Item             2015 price    2015 Spending
    Coffee (50 cups)      $2.00         $100.00
    Tea (50 cups)         $1.00          $50.00
    Scones (100)         $1.50         $150.00
     Total                              $300.00
                                                                                                        5-26
                                                                           26

•  Actually, consumer substitutes tea for coffee
   – Scone purchases constant
• True CPI for consumer is 250 / 200 = 1.25
• CPI estimate of 1.50 is 20% higher than the
  consumer’s true experience

 Item             2015 price    2015 Spending
 Coffee (00 cups)      $2.00           $0.00
 Tea (100 cups)        $1.00         $100.00
 Scones (100)         $1.50         $150.00
  Total                              $250.00
                                                                                                   5-27
                                                                       27

• Another important bias in the CPI is its
  measurement of price changes but not quality
  changes
   – PC with 20% more memory has 20% higher price
          • Not the same PC as the one from 10 years ago
   – If no adjustment is made for quality, PC's contribution
      to the CPI will be 20%
• Adjusting for quality is difficult
   – Large numbers of goods
   – Subjective differences
• Incorporating new goods is difficult
    (see next page)
                                                                          28

• Incorporating new goods is difficult
   – No base year price for this year's new goods
• When new goods become available, consumers
  can find products that more closely meet their
  needs
• New goods can only lower the cost of living, as
  consumers can choose not to buy them
• The CPI misses this effect because it uses a
  fixed basket of goods
• Thus, the CPI overstates any increases in the
  cost of living
                                                                       29

• The price level is a measure of the overall
  level of prices at a particular point in time
  – Measured by a price index such as the CPI
• The relative price of a specific good is a
  comparison of its price to the prices of other
  goods and services
• Suppose we have a one-time doubling of the
  gas price
   – Overall price level and inflation increase by a small
     amount
   – The increase in the relative price of gasoline is large                                                                                                     5-31
                                                                         31

• Relative prices can change significantly
  without corresponding changes in
  inflation
• E.g. summer prices
         Higher                Lower
  • Beach hotels          • Fresh fruit and
                             vegetables  • Cruises
                        • Heating oil  • Gas prices


                                                                                                   5-32
                                                                        32

Oil Price    Relative Price  Year     CPI       Inflation                            Change         of Oil
  2013     1.20
  2014     1.32     10%       8%          -2%
  2015     1.40     6%        8%        2%

• Government rarely attempts to manage
  relative prices
  – Can distort supply and demand for that
     industry

                                                                                                  5-33
                                                                       33

• Prices transmit information about
  – The cost of production and
  – The relationship between demand and supply in
     the market
• Inflation creates static (noise) in the
  communication
  – Buyers and sellers can't easily tell whether
         • The relative price of this good is increasing OR
         • Inflation is increasing the price of this good and all others
  – Deciding these issues requires market participants
     gather information – at a cost
  – Response to changing prices is tentative and slow5-34
                                                                           34

• Income taxes have been indexed to avoid
  bracket creep
  – Bracket creep occurs when a household is moved
      into a higher tax bracket due to increases in
    nominal but not real income
         • Higher tax brackets have a higher tax rate
• Indexing income taxes matches tax rates to
  the real income level
  – E.g. the tax rate on $50,000 is 25% in 2000
  – CPI is 1 for 2000, 1.25 for 2005
  – Nominal income of $62,500 is taxed 25% in 2005                                                                                                     5-35
                                                                         35

• However, not all taxes are indexed
• E.g. Capital depreciation allowance encourages
  purchase of capital goods
   – Allows firms to deduct a share of the purchase price of
    a new investment as a business expense
   – A new machine costs $1,000 and its useful life is 10
     years
          • U.S. tax law: Capital depreciation allowance of $100 per year
          • $100 in year 1 is worth more than $100 in year 10 because of
            inflation
•  In times of high inflation, the incentive of investment
   in new plant and equipment decreases
                                                                                                      5-36
                                                                          36

• A carpenter makes furniture using wood as input
    – Buys $160 of wood at the beginning of the year
    – Sells $200 of furniture at the end of the year
    – Earns $40 profits, owes $12 in taxes (30% tax rate)
Year    No Inflation 20% Inflation 60% Inflation
Cost         $160          $160          $160
Sales         $200          $240          $320
Profit         $40           $80           $160
Tax           $12           $24           $48
Tax (real)     $12      $24/1.2 = $20  $48/1.6 = $30
 •  Inflation causes profits to be overstated
    – Increases the real value of taxes owed
                                                                          37

•  If there is no inflation, cash holds its value over
  time
   – Some cash will be held for convenience
• When inflation is high, cash loses value over time
• People manage cash balances to limit losses
   – More frequent, smaller withdrawals cost consumers and
     businesses time, travel – a real cost of inflation
   – Banks process more transactions, increasing costs –
     another real cost of inflation
   – Costs of managing cash holding are called "shoe leather"
      costs, referring to the cost of frequent trips to the bank

                                                                                                      5-38
                                                                          38

• Unexpected inflation redistributes wealth
• Suppose workers' salaries are not indexed
  and inflation is higher than anticipated
  – Salaries lose purchasing power
  – Employers gain at the expense of workers
• Similarly, unexpectedly high inflation benefits
  borrowers at the expense of lenders
  – Borrowers repay with dollars worth less than
     anticipated
• Unexpected inflation confuses incentives
                                                                                                     5-39
                                                                         39

• Some decisions have a long time horizon
  – Erratic inflation makes planning risky
• E.g. retirement planning requires an
  estimated cost for your desired life-style
  – Save too little and you live less well in the future
  – Save too much and you live less well now
• Given the costs of inflation, most economists
  agree that low and stable inflation promotes a
  healthy economy
  – Most central banks target for a 2% inflation
                                                                                                     5-40
                                                                         40

•  Hyperinflation is an extremely high rate of inflation
   – In 1923, German employers paid workers twice a day (inflation
     was 102,000,000%)
   – Magnifies the costs of inflation
   – Minimize your cash holding
• A study of market economies, 1960 – 1996 showed 45
  episodes of high inflation (100+%) in 25 countries
   – Real GDP/person fell by an
      average of 1.6% per year
   – Real consumption/ person fell by
     an average of 1.3% per year
   – Real investment per person fell by
     an average of 3.3% per year                                                                                                       5-41
                                                                          41

• The effect of inflation on debtors and creditors can
  be explained more precisely using real interest rate
• The real interest rate is the annual percentage
  increase in the purchasing power of financial assets
   – Real cost of borrowing capital
   – Real interest rate = nominal interest rate – inflation
                    r = i - π
• The nominal interest rate is the annual
  percentage increase in the dollar value of an asset
   – Nominal interest rates are the most commonly stated
     rates
   – Not adjusted for inflation                                                  5-42
                                                                          42

• Nominal interest rates and

   • Nominal interest rate range is                                   1975     8.0%      9.1
   3.2% to 11.4%                                   1980      11.4       13.5
   • Inflation rate range is 1.6% to                                   1985     10.6        3.6
   13.5%                                   1990       8.6        5.4
•  Real interest rate is nominal                                   1995       6.6        2.8
   interest rate minus inflation                                   2000       6.0        3.4
   • Real interest rate was highest                                   2005       4.3        3.4
     in 1985, 7.0%                                   2010       3.2        1.6
   • Real interest rate was lowest
     in 1980, – 2.1%
                                                                                                        5-43
                                                                           43

• Unexpected inflation benefits borrowers and
  hurts lenders
  – For a given nominal interest rate, the higher the
      inflation rate, the lower the real interest rate
• Expected inflation may not hurt lenders if
  they can adjust the nominal interest rates
  – Inflation-protected bonds pay a real rate of
     interest plus the inflation rate
• The Fisher effect is the tendency for
  nominal interest rates to be high when
  inflation is high and low when inflation is low5-45
                                                                         45

the CPI was 118. Find the real rate of interest earned by
Albert in each of the three years and his total real return
over the three-year period. Assume that interest earnings
are reinvested each year and themselves earn interest.
